item_name: Guesstimate / market sizing (top-down, bottom-up, funnel, frequency x penetration, Fermi), PM interview and consulting (McKinsey/BCG/Bain) variants
what_interviewers_test: Across sources the question tests one ability: building a defensible number from scratch with no data, by breaking it into drivers you can estimate, stating and justifying assumptions, doing clean mental math, and checking whether the result is plausible. The exact number matters less than the process (CaseInterviewHub ex-McKinsey interviewers, 2026; StrategyCase 2026; HelloPM 2024; RocketBlocks ex-Google PM). Google (Product Analysis area): size impact quickly, sanity-check assumptions, and tie the estimate to a product or business decision. One interviewer account says it works as a proxy for causal, scientist-like thinking, not a math exercise (StellarPeers 2025; Blind comment Oct 2025; Julia Winn ex-Google interviewer, 2022/2024). Consulting (MBB): structuring, comfort with assumptions, mental math under pressure, communication and business judgment. Usually embedded inside a larger case rather than asked standalone (StrategyCase 2026; CaseInterviewHub 2026). India consumer tech (Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato): a screening-stage check of whether your logic is easy to follow and sanity-checked on India-scale consumer behaviour (orders, GMV, riders), often paired with a product case or RCA (The Product Folks 2025/26; Glassdoor Flipkart APM).
format_variants: 1) Standalone, candidate-led: the candidate owns clarify, structure, calculate, check and conclude. Typical time box 5-10 minutes (StrategyCase 2026). In India PM screens and Bain/BCG first rounds, a 10-15 minute block inside a 30-45 minute interview is common [uncertain]. 2) Embedded sizing step inside a market-entry or product case: 2-3 minutes, rounder numbers, faster closure expected (StrategyCase 2026). This is the McKinsey and interviewer-led pattern; McKinsey rarely or never asks a standalone sizing question (StrategyCase 2026; CaseInterviewHub 2026). 3) Google analytical / Product Analysis: about 35 minutes of core time covers about two questions with follow-ups, so an estimate gets about 10-15 minutes and is often followed by 'what metric would move' or 'is this worth building' (StellarPeers 2025; Julia Winn 2022). 4) Interviewer-led with supplied data: the interviewer hands out numbers. Grading then shifts away from grounding your own assumptions and toward using the data correctly and pushing back if a supplied number gives an implausible result (PrepLounge). 5) Take-home or written: rare for this type. Expect more precision, sourcing and a sensitivity table [uncertain]. In a text-only transcript grader, format is judged only from what the candidate says. The grader should infer the format from the prompt (standalone vs embedded) and scale time and depth expectations to match.

dimensions.name: Scoping and clarification
dimensions.definition: Pins down exactly what number is being estimated before any math: metric (units vs value, revenue vs GMV vs orders), geography, time period, inclusions and exclusions, and the purpose of the estimate.
dimensions.signal_sought: Avoids solving the wrong problem. Asks few, decision-relevant questions, or states scoping assumptions explicitly when the interviewer says 'you decide'.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the candidate's clarifying questions or scoping statements, e.g. 'Are we estimating daily orders or GMV?', 'I'll take Bangalore city only, food delivery only, excluding Instamart.' Absence of any scope statement before calculation is itself evidence.

dimensions.name: Approach and structure
dimensions.definition: Chooses a fitting decomposition (top-down population funnel, bottom-up supply or unit capacity, frequency x penetration, or a Fermi chain), states it out loud as an equation before plugging numbers, and keeps the tree short (2-3 levels).
dimensions.signal_sought: A logical, followable equation whose drivers multiply to the asked-for unit. The choice of method is justified (e.g. supply-side for a constrained market), and ideally a second method is named for triangulation.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the stated equation or plan, e.g. 'Daily orders = online-ordering households x orders per week / 7 x Swiggy share; I'll cross-check bottom-up from restaurants x orders per restaurant.' Note whether the structure was stated before numbers or emerged piecemeal.

dimensions.name: Segmentation (MECE where it matters)
dimensions.definition: Splits the population or supply into segments only where behaviour differs materially (city tier, age, income, heavy vs light users, B2B vs B2C). Segments are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, and each gets its own assumption.
dimensions.signal_sought: Segmentation that changes the answer, with no overlap or double counting. No cosmetic segmentation added to look rigorous (CaseInterviewHub 2026; RocketBlocks).
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the segments and why they were chosen, e.g. 'Splitting metros vs tier-2 because ordering frequency differs about 3x.' Flag overlaps, e.g. counting 'students' and '18-24 year olds' separately.

dimensions.name: Assumption grounding
dimensions.definition: Each numeric input is stated explicitly and justified with an anchor: known fact, personal or observed behaviour, analogy, or physical constraint. The candidate notes confidence in the input and avoids implausible numbers.
dimensions.signal_sought: Defensible, explained inputs ('because...'), not arbitrary averages. Recognises which inputs are weakest. Knows basic anchors (India about 1.4B, US about 340M) (CaseInterviewHub 2026; PMMockr 2026; RocketBlocks).
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote each assumption with its justification, e.g. 'About 35% of Bangalore orders online, roughly the smartphone-owning working-age share.' Count stated-but-unjustified numbers and obviously implausible ones (e.g. '90% of elderly post daily').

dimensions.name: Calculation accuracy and hygiene
dimensions.definition: Arithmetic is correct. Units and time periods are tracked at every step (per day vs per week, lakh/crore vs million/billion). Numbers are rounded sensibly to keep the math tractable without false precision.
dimensions.signal_sought: Correct intermediate and final arithmetic, visible units, and self-correction of slips. No order-of-magnitude errors.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Recompute every multiplication and division the candidate states and quote any incorrect line verbatim, e.g. '4.5M x 2 / 7 = 1.3M' (correct) vs '13M x 35% = 45M' (wrong by 10x). Quote unit conversions.

dimensions.name: Sanity check and sensitivity
dimensions.definition: Unprompted plausibility check of intermediate and final results against an independent anchor (per-capita ratio, known benchmark, second method), plus identification of the assumptions the answer is most sensitive to and the resulting range.
dimensions.signal_sought: The candidate catches their own errors before the interviewer does, triangulates, and gives a range ('500-700k'). Names the one or two biggest-swing assumptions (IGotAnOffer 2026; RocketBlocks; Julia Winn 2022; StrategyCase 2026).
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the check, e.g. 'That is about one order per 20 residents per day, which feels right for a metro'; 'Bottom-up gives 600k, close to 650k top-down'; 'Most sensitive to order frequency.' Record whether it was unprompted or followed an interviewer prompt.

dimensions.name: Communication and synthesis
dimensions.definition: Thinks out loud so every step is followable, checks in at key junctures, commits to a clear final number with units and range, and gives the 'so what' (what the number implies for the business or product decision).
dimensions.signal_sought: Answer-first close, a stated number rather than trailing off, and an implication tied to the purpose (e.g. 'so a 1% conversion lift is worth about X orders a day, worth pursuing'). (CaseInterviewHub 2026; StrategyCase 2026; PrepLounge; Julia Winn 2022.)
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the final statement and any implication sentence, and the check-ins ('Does this structure make sense before I plug in numbers?'). Note long unexplained jumps, e.g. a number appearing with no derivation.

weights.summary: No company or consulting firm publishes numeric weights for estimation questions. StrategyCase (ex-McKinsey) states explicitly that there is 'no fixed quota' across dimensions. All weights below are therefore inferred from how often and how strongly independent prep-platform and interviewer-account sources name each criterion. They are recommended weights, not observed ones.

recommended.reasoning: Named first by every source, both consulting and PM. CaseInterviewHub: 'the process matters more than the end result.' It carries the most weight because the other dimensions depend on it.

Every source names it ('comfort with assumptions', 'justify each assumption', 'unrealistic assumptions' listed as a top mistake). The Google interviewer account flags discomfort with estimating under limited information as the top Fermi failure.

recommended.provenance: inferred; consulting sources weight it higher, PM sources lower
recommended.reasoning: Consulting treats math errors as an 'Insufficient', which means automatic reject (StrategyCase feedback sheet). A Google PM account warns 'it's not a math exercise' (Blind 2025). Compromise: moderate weight, with a hard gate for uncorrected order-of-magnitude errors.

recommended.provenance: inferred (convergent; strongest agreement of any dimension after structure)
recommended.reasoning: IGotAnOffer calls the missing sense-check the most common mistake. Google's Product Analysis description explicitly includes 'sanity-check assumptions'. Weighted equal to math because catching your own errors is the observable trait interviewers praise.

'Stopping at the number' is called the most common soft fail (CaseInterviewHub). Thinking out loud is a precondition for every other score. Kept below the substantive dimensions so polished talk cannot carry a weak estimate.
Sources value it but warn against over-segmenting. It is partly a sub-skill of structure, so it gets a smaller separate weight.
Universally listed as step 1 but quick (about 60 seconds). Low weight, but a wrong-quantity error is handled by a gate.

weights.disagreements: 1) Math weight: consulting sources (StrategyCase, PrepLounge) treat arithmetic errors as near-disqualifying. PM sources (Blind Google account, HelloPM, Tear Them Down) say the process matters and minor slips are forgivable if caught. Resolution: 15% weight plus a gate only for uncorrected errors that change the order of magnitude. 2) The 'so what' / business implication: strongly emphasised by Google PM accounts (link to metrics or investment decision, Julia Winn) and MBB ('a raw number is not a recommendation', StrategyCase). Rarely mentioned by Indian PM prep sources, which stop at the sanity check (TPF, HelloPM). Kept inside Communication and synthesis, with level-based expectations. 3) Triangulation via a second method: described as a strong move by CaseInterviewHub and TPF, not required by IGotAnOffer. Treated as a level-4 anchor, not a requirement. 4) Accuracy tolerance: StrategyCase says within 10x is generally fine and within 25% is excellent. PrepLounge says ideally within 20%. Both agree that accuracy is secondary to logic.
weights.company_adjustments: Optional reweights, all inferred: Google: move about 5 points from Segmentation to Communication and synthesis (business implication). MBB/consulting: move about 5 points from Communication to Calculation accuracy. India consumer-tech screens: keep the base weights but require India-relevant segmentation (city tier, smartphone/UPI penetration, income) for a Segmentation score of 3 or higher [uncertain].

must_pass_gates.gate: Uncorrected order-of-magnitude arithmetic or unit error in the final answer (e.g. per-day vs per-year, lakh vs million slip) that the candidate never catches
must_pass_gates.source: StrategyCase feedback sheet: 'math errors' map to Insufficient, an automatic reject (https://strategycase.com/case-interview-feedback-sheet/). Softened from reject to a cap for PM context (inferred).

must_pass_gates.gate: Accepts an implausible result without questioning it (e.g. more units than people, Julia Winn's 'trillion dollars from offline downloads' example)
must_pass_gates.cap: Overall max Lean Hire (2.5/4) and Sanity check scored 1
must_pass_gates.source: Julia Winn, ex-Google interviewer (https://medium.com/@4thewinn/the-google-pm-analytical-interview-the-most-common-mistakes-6dc269f940a6); CaseInterviewHub 2026; PrepLounge (objecting to implausible interviewer-supplied inputs).

must_pass_gates.gate: No final number committed (trails off, or asks the interviewer whether it is right without stating an answer)
must_pass_gates.source: CaseInterviewHub ('stopping at the number' soft fail; never recite and stop); IGotAnOffer (candidates who look up expecting validation); Tripathi failure account (trailed off, not hired).

must_pass_gates.gate: No structure stated: jumps straight into multiplying numbers with no equation or plan visible in the transcript
must_pass_gates.cap: Approach and structure max 2; overall max Lean Hire
must_pass_gates.source: IGotAnOffer MBB market sizing ('jumping straight into calculations without first organizing your thoughts'); StrategyCase ('no real structure' maps to Insufficient).

must_pass_gates.gate: Estimated the wrong quantity (e.g. sized market revenue when asked for orders, or the whole country when asked for one city) and did not reconcile it
must_pass_gates.source: CaseInterviewHub ('getting this wrong is the fastest way to waste four minutes on the wrong number'); inferred cap.

must_pass_gates.gate: Interviewer had to supply the structure or repeatedly rescue the candidate (heavy prompting)
must_pass_gates.source: StrategyCase feedback sheet: 'needed heavy prompting' maps to Adequate, 'reject in almost every case'.

must_pass_gates.gate: Inputs given with no derivation at all (a 'black box' answer), so reasoning is not observable
must_pass_gates.cap: Assumption grounding max 1; overall max Lean No Hire
must_pass_gates.source: PMMockr 2026 ('interviewer cannot follow or critique your reasoning... appears arbitrary'); PrepLounge ('interviewers cannot read your mind').

Scoping and clarification.1: Starts calculating immediately. The quantity is ambiguous or wrong (e.g. asked daily orders, sizes annual GMV). No scope statement.
Scoping and clarification.2: Asks generic or excessive questions ('What's the population?' 'Can you give me data?') or clarifies only one axis. Scope is stated vaguely.
Scoping and clarification.3: Confirms metric, geography and time period in 1-3 crisp questions or explicit statements: 'Daily orders, Bangalore city, food delivery only. I'll exclude grocery.'
Scoping and clarification.4: As 3, plus ties scope to the purpose of the estimate and declares exclusions that change the answer: 'If this is for rider capacity planning I'll size peak-hour orders, not the daily average. Is that the goal?'

Approach and structure.1: No visible method. Numbers appear in sequence with no equation. The method cannot produce the asked-for unit.
Approach and structure.2: A generic population x percentage chain with a missing or mis-specified driver (e.g. no frequency term). The structure is recited without saying why it fits.
Approach and structure.3: States a correct driver equation before plugging in numbers, 2-3 levels deep, with the method choice justified: 'I'll go top-down from households since ordering is a household behaviour.'
Approach and structure.4: As 3, plus picks the most informative lens (e.g. supply-side for a capacity-constrained market) and names a second method for triangulation: 'Top-down first, then bottom-up from restaurants x orders per outlet to cross-check.'

Segmentation (MECE where it matters).1: No segmentation where behaviour clearly differs (e.g. one average for metro and rural India), or segments overlap and double count.
Segmentation (MECE where it matters).2: Segments are listed but cosmetic: the same assumption is applied to each, or segmentation adds steps without changing the answer.
Segmentation (MECE where it matters).3: 2-4 MECE segments chosen because behaviour differs, each with its own assumption: 'Metro heavy users about 3 orders/week, tier-2 about 1/week.'
Segmentation (MECE where it matters).4: As 3, plus explains why this cut is the most decision-relevant and checks exhaustiveness: 'Students, working professionals and families cover all urban adults; I'm leaving out under-15s because they don't order themselves.'

Assumption grounding.1: Numbers stated without justification, or clearly implausible ('90% of Indians order food online weekly'). Wrong basic anchors (India population '500 million').
Assumption grounding.2: Most numbers are plausible but justified only with 'I think' or 'let's say'. Confidence in individual inputs is not flagged.
Assumption grounding.3: Each key input has an explicit anchor (known fact, observed behaviour, analogy): 'About 35%, roughly the share of the city with a smartphone and disposable income.' Correct basic anchors.
Assumption grounding.4: As 3, plus explicitly ranks which assumptions are weakest and highest-impact and invites correction: 'Order frequency is my shakiest input and drives the answer most. Do you have a view, or shall I proceed at 2 per week?'

Calculation accuracy and hygiene.1: An order-of-magnitude or unit error survives to the final answer (per-week treated as per-day, lakh/million confusion).
Calculation accuracy and hygiene.2: Minor arithmetic slips, some caught only after the interviewer prompts. Units dropped at some steps. Rounding is either excessive or falsely precise (e.g. carrying 337.2M).
Calculation accuracy and hygiene.3: Arithmetic correct throughout. Units and time period are stated at each step. Rounding is sensible: '13M x 35% is about 4.5M people.'
Calculation accuracy and hygiene.4: As 3, plus fast, clean mental math with self-correction narrated ('wait, that's weekly, divide by 7: about 650k a day') and handling of messy numbers by rounding in compensating directions.

Sanity check and sensitivity.1: No check. Accepts an implausible result, or checks only when the interviewer asks 'does that sound right?'
Sanity check and sensitivity.2: A token check ('seems reasonable') with no anchor, or a check made only after prompting.
Sanity check and sensitivity.3: An unprompted check against an independent anchor or per-capita ratio: 'That's about one order per 20 residents a day, plausible for a metro.' Gives a range.
Sanity check and sensitivity.4: As 3, plus triangulates with a second method, names the one or two most sensitive assumptions with their effect on the range, and states what data would refine it: 'Bottom-up gives 600k vs 650k top-down. ±30% on frequency moves it 450-850k. I'd validate frequency with cohort data.'

Communication and synthesis.1: Long silences or unexplained jumps, no final number, or ends with 'Is that right?'
Communication and synthesis.2: Explains steps but rambles or loses the thread. The final number is stated without units or range, with no implication.
Communication and synthesis.3: Followable think-aloud, at least one check-in at the structure stage, and a clear final answer with units and range: 'So about 650k orders a day, likely 500-700k.'
Communication and synthesis.4: As 3, plus answer-first summary and a 'so what' tied to the purpose: 'about 650k a day, so a 2% conversion lift is about 13k orders a day, worth an experiment', delivered concisely.

level_expectations: Anchors are the same across levels, but what counts as 'solid' (3) shifts [inferred; no source publishes level-specific estimation anchors]. APM / new grad (Flipkart APM, Google APM, campus PM): 3 means correct scope, a stated equation, grounded assumptions, correct math and an unprompted sanity check. The 'so what' and triangulation are bonus (4-level). Moderate nudging on structure is tolerated once. India campus APM screens lean heavily on guesstimates plus RCA as filters (Ananya Malhotra Flipkart APM accounts, 2020, background only; Glassdoor Flipkart APM). PM (L4-L5 / mid-level): 3 additionally needs purpose-aware scoping, segmentation that changes the answer, and naming the most sensitive assumption. A business implication is expected when the prompt has a product context (Julia Winn's Google analytical format links the estimate to behaviour change, metrics and investment worthiness). Senior PM (L6+): estimation is rarely standalone. It is folded into strategy or 'is this worth building' questions. 3 requires the candidate to frame the estimate around the decision (TAM vs SAM vs obtainable, or capacity vs demand), keep the math brief, and spend time on implications, risks and what data would change the call. Over-investing in arithmetic precision at senior level reads as missing judgment (Blind Google L6 thread, Oct 2025: 'operate like a scientist, not just a calculator'). Consulting analogue: undergrad/MBA candidates are held to the 'Good vs Very Good' line on quant reasoning. 'Distinctive' needs the business implication without prompting (StrategyCase).
green_flags: States the exact quantity, unit, geography and period before calculating ('daily orders, Bangalore, food only').
Writes or speaks the driver equation first, then fills it in; names top-down vs bottom-up and why.
Justifies each input with an anchor ('about 250 working days', 'roughly the smartphone-owning share') and flags the shakiest one.
Segments only where behaviour differs, e.g. metro vs tier-2 ordering frequency, heavy vs light users.
Narrates self-corrections on units or arithmetic before the interviewer notices.
Runs an unprompted per-capita or second-method sanity check and gives a range.
Closes answer-first with the number, the range and a one-line 'so what' for the business or product decision.
Uses the interviewer's hint or supplied data immediately and correctly, and objects if a supplied number produces an implausible result (PrepLounge).
red_flags: Recites a memorised template ('population, then percentage, then frequency, then price') without adapting it to the question. Memorising frameworks instead of thinking is StrategyCase's #1 mistake.
Multiplies the full population by an average rate, ignoring non-users (PMMockr 2026).
Unstated or arbitrary assumptions; numbers appear with no derivation.
Over-segmentation or decimals that add steps without changing the answer (false precision, e.g. 337.2M).
Spends most of the time on a sub-estimate that barely affects the total (Julia Winn).
Never sanity-checks, or accepts an absurd result as reasonable.
Freezes or asks for data instead of estimating ('I don't know the population, can you tell me?'). This is discomfort with uncertainty (Julia Winn; Tripathi account).
Trails off without a final number, or ends with 'Is that correct?'
recitation_vs_insight: Recitation looks like a generic chain (population x % online x frequency x share) delivered in the same order for any prompt, with segment labels but identical assumptions per segment, 'let's assume' numbers with no anchor, and a closing 'seems reasonable' with no comparison. Insight shows up in: (a) a structure chosen for this market's binding constraint (e.g. supply-side for quick-commerce dark-store capacity, frequency x penetration for a habitual service); (b) segments whose assumptions differ, with a stated reason; (c) awareness of which input dominates the answer; (d) a sanity check using an independent anchor or second method that could actually disagree; (e) a so-what tied to the purpose. Grader tests: 1) If you swapped the product name, would the answer be unchanged? If yes, it is recitation and Approach caps at 2. 2) Does every segment have a distinct, justified number? If not, Segmentation caps at 2. 3) Does the sanity check compare against something outside the candidate's own chain? If not, Sanity check caps at 2. 4) Is the most sensitive assumption named? Without it, no 4 on Assumption grounding or Sanity check. Source basis: StrategyCase ('memorizing frameworks instead of thinking', 'picking the wrong structure'); CaseInterviewHub ('segmenting where it does not [matter]' is a listed mistake); RocketBlocks (differentiated assumptions per segment). The tests themselves are inferred.
process_signals: Clarifying questions: 1-3 targeted questions on metric, geography, period and purpose are ideal. Zero is acceptable only if scope is stated explicitly as assumptions. More than 4, or requests for data the candidate should estimate (population, city size), count against Scoping and Assumption grounding (IGotAnOffer: clarify 'exactly what number'; CaseTutor: about 60 seconds). Check-ins: one check-in after stating the structure is a green flag (CaseInterviewHub; Tripathi 'invite pushback'). Checking in after every number is padding. Use of interviewer data: once a number is supplied, the candidate must use it, not keep their own. If a supplied number yields an implausible result, the strong move is to say so (PrepLounge). Credit only what the candidate does with the data; never credit the data itself. Hints: if the interviewer answers 'what do you think?', the candidate should treat it as a cue to assume and move on (Tear Them Down 2022). Hint penalty (inferred; no source gives numbers): a minor nudge (e.g. 'what about frequency?') lowers the affected dimension by up to 1 point. Interviewer-supplied structure or a caught error the candidate missed caps that dimension at 2. Two or more rescues trigger the heavy-prompting gate (max Lean Hire, per StrategyCase 'needed heavy prompting'). Pushback: when challenged on an assumption, strong candidates defend it with the anchor or update it with the recalculated result. Weak candidates either capitulate with no reasoning or ignore the challenge.
time_allocation: Standalone 8-12 minute estimate (StrategyCase: 5-10 min; Google about 10-15 min per question within a 35-min core block, StellarPeers): scope 0.5-1 min (about 10%), structure 1-2 min (about 15%), assumptions and math 4-6 min (about 50%), sanity check and range 1-2 min (about 15%), conclusion and so-what 0.5-1 min (about 10%). Embedded sizing inside a case: 2-3 minutes total, rounder numbers (StrategyCase). Penalties (inferred): running out of time before stating a final number triggers the 'no final number' gate. Spending more than 50% of the time on scoping or structure before any number lowers Communication by 1. A sanity check skipped for lack of time scores Sanity check 1, since a 20-second per-capita check is always possible. In a transcript grader, approximate time by the share of turns or words per phase when timestamps are absent.
hire_thresholds: No company publishes a guesstimate-specific hire mapping. Recommended mapping on the weighted 1-4 score, after applying gates (inferred, calibrated to StrategyCase's MBB scale, where 'Good' is borderline and 'Very Good' is offer territory, and to the consulting norm that one Insufficient sinks the case): Strong Hire: weighted score ≥3.5, no dimension below 3, Sanity check and Structure both 4. Hire: ≥3.0, no dimension below 2, Structure ≥3, Sanity check ≥3, no gate triggered. Lean Hire: 2.5-2.99, or ≥3.0 with one gate capping at Lean Hire. Lean No Hire: 2.0-2.49, or any Lean No Hire gate. No Hire: <2.0, or two or more dimensions at 1. Company and level differences: MBB is the strictest on math. Any uncorrected arithmetic error is effectively a reject there (StrategyCase), so in consulting mode make Calculation=1 a hard No Hire. Google evaluates estimation inside Product Analysis among several areas, so one weak estimate can be offset elsewhere in the loop, but within the question the bar includes the business implication (StellarPeers; Julia Winn). Indian APM campus screens are relative or comparative ('selection process is apparently relative', Flipkart APM account, 2020 background), so thresholds there act more like a ranking than a fixed bar [uncertain]. Senior levels: require Communication and synthesis ≥3 for Hire, since the decision link is expected.
company_differences: Google: estimation sits within the Product Analysis area (formerly Analytical), alongside root-cause analysis. Expect to 'size impact, sanity-check assumptions', often extended into metrics or investment-worthiness (StellarPeers 2025/26; Julia Winn ex-Google interviewer 2022/2024). Classic Google prompts: time at stop lights, Gmail messages per second (IGotAnOffer). One L6 account says math alone does not pass the round (Blind 2025). Meta: no dedicated estimation round in the current PM loop (Product Sense, Analytical Thinking/Execution, Leadership). Estimation appears only embedded, e.g. sizing impact within an analytical-thinking question [uncertain]. Amazon: IGotAnOffer data indicates Amazon 'tends not to' ask estimation questions compared with Google and Facebook. That source is about Amazon program manager roles, so applying it to PM roles is [uncertain]. Amazon's emphasis is LP behavioural plus data-driven judgment. Microsoft: estimation is occasionally asked in PM loops but is not a defining round [uncertain]. Uber: two-sided marketplace estimation (riders, drivers, trips per city) is reported in prep material, but no grading-specific source was found [uncertain]. India consumer tech: Flipkart APM first rounds combine a product case or RCA with a guesstimate (Glassdoor Flipkart APM; Malhotra 2020 account). Swiggy, Zomato and Flipkart guesstimates are India-specific (orders per day in a city, festive-season GMV). The interviewer watches whether 'your logic is easy to follow and sanity-checked' (The Product Folks). India-specific bar differences (inferred from Indian prep platforms, not confirmed by interviewers): expect India-relevant segmentation (city tier, income band, smartphone/UPI/internet penetration, joint vs nuclear households), comfort with lakh/crore units, and top-down plus bottom-up triangulation (TPF's worked Swiggy example does both). Guesstimates are used more as screening filters at Indian companies than at US big tech [uncertain]. PhonePe and Meesho: no grading-specific source found; Meesho prompts likely focus on tier-2/3 and reseller behaviour [uncertain]. Consulting: McKinsey does not ask standalone sizing (embedded only). Bain often includes dedicated market sizing in early rounds. BCG is mixed (StrategyCase 2026; CaseInterviewHub 2026).

calibration_exemplars.prompt: Estimate the number of food-delivery orders Swiggy fulfils in Bangalore on a weekday.
calibration_exemplars.score_1: Candidate says 'Bangalore has maybe 1 crore people, say half order every day, so 50 lakh orders, Swiggy has maybe 60%, so 30 lakh.' No scope, no frequency term (assumes daily ordering), no justification, no check, and accepts that about 30% of the city orders Swiggy daily. Gates: implausible result accepted; no structure.
calibration_exemplars.score_2: States 'population x % who order online x orders per week / 7 x Swiggy share', but uses 'let's say' numbers with no anchors, lists segments (students, professionals, families) with the same frequency for each, makes one unit slip caught only after the interviewer asks 'per day or per week?', and ends with 'so about 9 lakh, does that sound right?' with no range or check.
calibration_exemplars.score_3: Confirms weekday, Bangalore city, food only. States the top-down equation. Splits heavy (young professionals, about 3/week) vs occasional users (about 0.5/week) with reasons. Anchors on about 1.3 crore population and smartphone/disposable-income share. Math is correct with units. Checks unprompted: 'about 650k a day is one order per 20 residents, plausible.' Gives a 5-7 lakh range and names order frequency as the most sensitive input.
calibration_exemplars.score_4: Everything in 3, plus asks the purpose ('rider planning or market share?'), triangulates bottom-up (about 20k active restaurants x about 30 Swiggy orders per day, about 6 lakh), reconciles the two methods, shows how ±30% on frequency moves the range, and closes answer-first with a so-what: 'about 6.5 lakh a day; if the goal is lunch-peak rider capacity, roughly 35% falls in a 2-hour window, so plan for about 2.3 lakh orders in that window.' Concise, with one check-in after the structure.

coachable_feedback.Scoping and clarification: Before any number, say one sentence that fixes metric, place, period and exclusions ('I'll estimate X per Y in Z, excluding W'). Practise it on 10 prompts until it takes under 30 seconds.
coachable_feedback.Approach and structure: Say the full driver equation out loud before plugging in any number, then say why that decomposition fits this market (demand-side vs supply-side).
coachable_feedback.Segmentation (MECE where it matters): Only split a segment if you can state a different number for it. For each segment, say 'this group differs because...' and drop any segment that gets the same assumption.
coachable_feedback.Assumption grounding: Attach a 'because' to every number (fact, observed behaviour or analogy), and at the end name your shakiest, highest-impact assumption.
coachable_feedback.Calculation accuracy and hygiene: Say the unit with every intermediate result ('4.5M people', '1.3M orders per day') and round to 1-2 significant figures. Drill lakh/crore to million/billion conversions.
coachable_feedback.Sanity check and sensitivity: End every estimate with a per-capita or second-method check plus a range, e.g. 'that's one per N people per day; bottom-up gives X; range A-B, most sensitive to C.'
coachable_feedback.Communication and synthesis: Close answer-first: number, range, then one sentence on what it means for the decision. Never end with 'is that right?'

llm_grading_notes: 1) Recompute the math: an 8B model tends to trust stated arithmetic. Instruct the grader to recompute every product or quotient and quote incorrect lines verbatim, or pre-compute them with a deterministic Python pass that extracts number expressions from the transcript and flags mismatches over 15% before the LLM scores. 2) Attribution: credit only numbers, structure and checks the candidate produced. If the interviewer supplied the structure, a data point or the sanity check, the grader must not credit it. Separate speaker turns and require evidence quotes from candidate turns only. 3) Length bias: long transcripts with many segments look rigorous. Apply the recitation tests (swap-the-product test, distinct-number-per-segment test) and cap scores where they fail. Reward concision at equal quality. 4) Leniency and central tendency: small models over-assign 3s. Require a quoted transcript span for every score of 3 or higher, and default to 2 if no quote satisfies the 3-anchor. 5) Accuracy vs reasonableness: do not penalise distance from a 'true' value the grader believes it knows (its own facts about Swiggy volumes may be wrong). Judge plausibility of the anchors and the internal consistency. Penalise only absurd anchors (India population off by 3x or more). 6) Prompt-induced checks: distinguish 'unprompted' from 'after interviewer asked' sanity checks. Only unprompted checks can score 3 or higher. 7) Gates first: evaluate must-pass gates before dimension scoring and apply caps after the weighted sum. Output the gate decisions explicitly. 8) Units: lakh/crore and per-day/per-week confusion is common in Indian transcripts. Ask the grader to normalise all numbers to a single unit table before judging. 9) Hallucinated evidence: require exact quotes and verify, by substring match in code, that each quote exists in the transcript. 10) Use the four calibration exemplars as few-shot examples, but vary the prompt domain so the grader does not anchor on Swiggy-specific numbers.
